title: UNIT 5: MATHEMATICAL APPLICATIONS IN BUSINESS
notes: ✓ Business mathematics → application of mathematical ideas to business activities and personal finance.

title: 5.1 BASIC MATHEMATICAL CONCEPTS IN BUSINESS
notes:
The basic concepts used in business calculations include:

◆ Ratio
◆ Rate
◆ Proportion
◆ Percentage
◆ Markup
◆ Discount
◆ Commission

These concepts are widely used in buying and selling, pricing, taxation and business transactions.

title: RATIO
notes:
✓ Ratio → comparison of two quantities of the same kind.

Ratio of a to b:
a:b = a/b

Ratios should normally be expressed in their simplest form.

Before comparing quantities with different units, convert them to the same unit.

◆ Business uses → comparing quantities, costs, production, sales and mixtures.

title: RATE
notes:
✓ Rate → comparison of two quantities having different units.

Examples:
◆ Birr per hour
◆ Kilometers per hour
◆ Birr per kilogram
◆ Interest per year

Rate tells how much of one quantity corresponds to one unit of another quantity.

title: RATE OF CHANGE
notes:
✓ Rate of change → measures how much one quantity changes relative to the change in another quantity.

Rate of change = Change in quantity / Change in corresponding quantity

Example → change in revenue per additional product sold.

→ Positive rate → quantity increases.
→ Negative rate → quantity decreases.

title: 5.1.3 PROPORTION
notes:
✓ Proportion → an equation stating that two ratios are equal.

If a/b = c/d, then:
ad = bc

→ Direct variation → y = kx.
→ Inverse variation → y = k/x.

Proportions are useful for solving business problems involving prices, quantities, wages, production and mixtures.

title: 5.1.4 PERCENTAGE
notes:
✓ Percentage → a ratio expressed per hundred.

x% = x/100

Percentage amount = Base × Rate

Rate = Percentage amount / Base

Base = Percentage amount / Rate

Percentages are used in discounts, commissions, markup, profit, loss and taxes.

title: MARKUP
notes:
✓ Markup → the difference between the selling price and the cost of a product.

Markup = Selling Price − Cost Price

Markup based on cost:
Markup % = (Markup / Cost Price) × 100%

Markup based on selling price:
Markup % = (Markup / Selling Price) × 100%

A business adds markup to make a profit from selling a product.

title: DISCOUNT
notes:
✓ Discount → reduction from the original or regular price of an item.

Discount = Original Price − Selling Price

Discount % = (Discount / Original Price) × 100%

Selling Price = Original Price − Discount

If discount rate is r:
Selling Price = Original Price × (1 − r)

title: 5.2 TIME VALUE OF MONEY
notes:
✓ Time value of money → the idea that a sum of money available today can have a different value from the same nominal amount available in the future because money can earn interest.

◆ Principal (P) → original amount invested or borrowed.
◆ Interest (I) → amount earned or paid for the use of money.
◆ Future value / Amount (A) → principal plus accumulated interest.
◆ Rate (r) → interest rate per period or year.
◆ Term (t) → length of time.

title: 5.2.1 SIMPLE INTEREST
notes:
✓ Simple interest → interest calculated only on the original principal throughout the term.

Formula:
I = Prt

Where:
P → principal
r → annual interest rate as a decimal
t → time in years

Future value:
A = P + I
A = P(1 + rt)

→ Interest does not earn additional interest under simple interest.

title: SIMPLE INTEREST: TIME
notes:
When time is given in months or days, convert it appropriately to the time unit used by the interest rate.

If time is in months:
t = months / 12

If time is in days using a 365-day year:
t = days / 365

→ Always make the rate and time compatible before applying I = Prt.

title: 5.2.2 COMPOUND INTEREST
notes:
✓ Compound interest → interest calculated on the principal plus previously accumulated interest.

If interest is compounded once per year:
A = P(1 + r)^t

If compounded m times per year:
A = P(1 + r/m)^(mt)

Compound interest:
CI = A − P

→ More frequent compounding generally produces a larger accumulated amount when the nominal rate and time are fixed.

title: COMPOUNDING FREQUENCY
notes:
◆ Annually → m = 1
◆ Semi-annually → m = 2
◆ Quarterly → m = 4
◆ Monthly → m = 12
◆ Daily → m = 365

The compounding frequency determines how many times interest is added during one year.

title: NOMINAL & EFFECTIVE INTEREST RATE
notes:
✓ Nominal rate → stated annual rate used with a specified compounding frequency.

✓ Effective annual rate (EAR) → annually compounded rate producing the same result as a given nominal rate and compounding frequency.

EAR = (1 + r/m)^m − 1

→ Effective rate is useful when comparing investments with different compounding frequencies.

title: 5.2.3 ANNUITY
notes:
✓ Annuity → a series of equal payments made at regular intervals.

Examples →
◆ Regular deposits into a savings account
◆ Mortgage payments
◆ Car-loan payments
◆ Pension payments
◆ Regular rent payments

Present value → value of the annuity at the beginning.
Future value → accumulated value at a future date.

title: TYPES OF ANNUITY
notes:
→ Ordinary annuity → payments are made at the end of each payment period.

→ Annuity due → payments are made at the beginning of each payment period.

The timing of the payments affects the accumulated value and present value of the annuity.

title: FUTURE VALUE OF ORDINARY ANNUITY
notes:
For equal periodic payment R, interest rate i per payment period and n payments:

Future Value:
FV = R[(1 + i)^n − 1] / i

R → periodic payment
i → interest rate per payment period
n → number of payments

→ Used for regular saving and investment deposits.

title: PRESENT VALUE OF ORDINARY ANNUITY
notes:
Present Value:
PV = R[1 − (1 + i)^(-n)] / i

Where:
R → periodic payment
i → interest rate per payment period
n → number of payments

→ Used to determine the current value of a series of future equal payments, such as loan or mortgage payments.

title: 5.2.4 AMORTIZATION
notes:
✓ Amortization → gradual repayment of a loan through a series of scheduled payments.

An amortization schedule shows:
1. Beginning loan balance
2. Payment
3. Interest portion
4. Principal portion
5. Ending balance

→ Each payment covers interest and reduces the outstanding principal.

title: AMORTIZATION PAYMENT
notes:
For a loan with present value PV, periodic interest rate i and n equal payments:

Payment:
R = PV × i / [1 − (1 + i)^(-n)]

Interest for a period:
Interest = Beginning Balance × i

Principal paid:
Principal Payment = Total Payment − Interest

New balance:
Ending Balance = Beginning Balance − Principal Payment

title: 5.2.5 DEPRECIATION
notes:
✓ Depreciation → decrease in the value of a fixed asset over time because of use, age or other factors.

◆ Initial cost → original purchase price.
◆ Useful life → expected period of use.
◆ Salvage/residual value → estimated value at the end of useful life.

The textbook develops two methods:
◆ Declining-balance depreciation
◆ Straight-line depreciation.

title: DECLINING-BALANCE DEPRECIATION
notes:
✓ Declining-balance depreciation → depreciation is calculated as a fixed percentage of the asset's decreasing value.

Depreciation for a period = Beginning Value × Depreciation Rate

Ending Value = Beginning Value − Depreciation

→ Because the depreciation rate is applied to a decreasing balance, the depreciation amount becomes smaller over time.

title: STRAIGHT-LINE DEPRECIATION
notes:
✓ Straight-line depreciation → the asset loses the same amount of value each year.

Annual depreciation:
D = (Cost − Salvage Value) / Useful Life

Book/depreciated value after t years:
V = Cost − tD

→ The annual depreciation amount remains constant throughout the useful life.

title: 5.3 SAVING, INVESTING AND FINANCING
notes:
→ Saving → setting aside money for future use.

→ Investing → putting money into an asset or activity with the expectation of earning a return.

→ Financing → obtaining funds for business activities, purchases or investments.

Main topics → Saving Money, Investment and Financing/Borrowing Money.

title: 5.3.2 INVESTMENT
notes:
✓ Investment → use of money or capital with the expectation of obtaining future income or profit.

A business can be organized in different forms, including sole proprietorship.
Investment choices discussed include stocks and bonds.

→ The purpose of investment is to make money work toward future financial goals.

title: STOCK / EQUITY
notes:
✓ Stock → ownership interest in a company.

A shareholder owns a fraction of the company represented by shares.
Shareholders may have voting rights.
Shareholders may receive dividends when declared.

Types discussed include:
◆ Authorized stock → maximum shares a company may issue.
◆ Issued stock → shares actually issued by the company.
◆ Outstanding stock → shares currently held by stockholders.

title: BONDS
notes:
✓ Bond → a debt instrument through which an investor lends money to an issuer.

◆ Face/par value → amount used as the reference value for interest payments.
◆ Coupon rate → stated interest rate on the bond's face value.
◆ Coupon payment → periodic interest payment.
◆ Maturity date → date when the bond reaches the end of its term.

→ Bonds provide interest income to investors according to their terms.

title: 5.4 TAXATION
notes:
✓ Taxation → compulsory payment by individuals and businesses to the government.

Taxes help the government finance services and activities such as:
◆ Education
◆ Health
◆ Defense
◆ Law and order
◆ Infrastructure and administration

Other objectives include:
◆ Reducing inequality
◆ Promoting economic stability
◆ Changing behavior
◆ Promoting economic growth
◆ Allocating resources.

title: DIRECT & INDIRECT TAXES
notes:
✓ Direct tax → tax whose impact and incidence generally fall on the person responsible for paying it.

Examples → employment income tax, business income tax and other income-based taxes.

✓ Indirect tax → tax whose burden can be passed to another person, commonly the consumer.

Examples → VAT, turnover tax, excise tax, customs duty and stamp duty.

title: 5.4.1 DIRECT TAXES
notes:
Direct taxes discussed include income-based taxes.

Sources of taxable income include:
◆ Employment income
◆ Rental income
◆ Business income
◆ Dividends
◆ Interest income
◆ Royalties
◆ Gains from investment assets
◆ Other specified income.

→ The textbook organizes income taxation under Schedules A, B, C and D.

title: UNIT 5 KEY FORMULAS
notes:
Percentage:
Percentage = Base × Rate

Simple interest:
I = Prt

Simple-interest amount:
A = P(1 + rt)

Compound amount:
A = P(1 + r/m)^(mt)

Compound interest:
CI = A − P

Effective annual rate:
EAR = (1 + r/m)^m − 1

Future value of ordinary annuity:
FV = R[(1+i)^n − 1]/i

Present value of ordinary annuity:
PV = R[1 − (1+i)^(-n)]/i

Loan payment:
R = PV × i/[1 − (1+i)^(-n)]

Straight-line depreciation:
D = (Cost − Salvage Value)/Useful Life

Depreciated value:
V = Cost − tD

Declining-balance depreciation:
Depreciation = Beginning Value × Depreciation Rate

Markup:
Markup = Selling Price − Cost Price

Discount:
Discount = Original Price − Selling Price

Commission:
Commission = Sales × Commission Rate

Employment income tax:
Tax = Taxable Income × Tax Rate − Deduction

title: QUICK EXAM REMINDER
notes:
→ Ratio → compares quantities of the same kind.

→ Rate → compares quantities with different units.

→ Proportion → two equal ratios.

→ Percentage → per hundred.

→ Markup → Selling Price − Cost.

→ Discount → Original Price − Selling Price.

→ Simple interest → calculated on principal only.

→ Compound interest → interest earns interest.

→ Annuity → equal payments at regular intervals.

→ Amortization → gradual repayment of a loan.

→ Depreciation → decrease in asset value.

→ Saving → setting money aside for future use.

→ Investment → putting money into something expected to produce a return.

→ Financing → obtaining funds for business activities.

→ Direct tax → burden generally falls on the taxpayer.

→ Indirect tax → burden can be passed to another person, commonly the consumer.

VAT, TOT, excise tax, customs duty and stamp duty → major indirect taxes discussed in the unit.
